A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Enjoys the company of others and seeks contact with others from birth.
• Shows their readiness to be social through using their sensory abilities; following movement and gazing at faces intently.
• Moves body, arms and legs and changes facial expression in response to others, e.g. sticking out tongue .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Offer warm, loving and consistent care in your interactions with babies and young children.
• Respond sensitively and quickly to babies and young children's needs.
• Learn from parents regarding caring practices at home .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• The setting offers a welcoming, calm, caring environment.
• Implement a Key Person Approach.
• Develop close partnerships with parents/carers.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Begins to display attachment behaviours such as wanting to stay near.
• Becomes wary of unfamiliar people.
• Draws others into social interaction through calling, crying and babbling .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Use care events to build a close relationship with babies and young children.
• Be physically and emotionally available to babies and young children to provide a secure base.
• Get to know each babies and young child's separation rituals .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Arrange for staff absence to be covered by practitioners who are already familiar to the children.
• Allocate a secondary key person who takes responsibility for the care of babies when their key person is absent.
• The day is predictable enough to give babies a sense of security but is flexible enough to respond to individual patterns.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Displays attachment behaviours such as wanting to stay near to their close carers.
• Explores confidently when they feel secure in the presence of a familiar adult.
• Closely watches others' body language to begin to understand their intentions .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Let your key children know where you are going, what you are doing and who they will be with.
• Support babies and young children's need to hold on to their special comfort object.
• Enable children to explore by being a secure base for them .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• The environment is designed so that the number of times the key person has to leave the room is limited.
• Group rooms are as home-like as possible and decorated with photographs of the children's families.
• Develop play opportunities centred on objects babies bring from home.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Builds relationships with special people but may show anxiety in the presence of strangers.
• Is becoming more able to separate from their close carers and explore new situations with support.
• Shows some understanding that other people have perspectives, ideas and needs that are different to theirs .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Use mealtimes as ideal occasions for children to practice social skills.
• Play name games to welcome children to the setting.
• Soothe each of your key children to sleep in the way agreed with their parent .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Provide duplicates of favourite items to reduce competition and conflict.
• Provide matching items for children and adults to mirror each other in play.
• Provide resources that promote cooperative play between two children.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Shows empathy and concern for people who are special to them.
• Seeks out others to share experiences with and may choose to play with a familiar friend.
• Shows increasing consideration of other people's needs and gradually more impulse control .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Offer a warm and consistent presence, spending time playing and being with children.
• Show that you keep children 'in mind' by referring to things you noticed in their play.
• Model key skills of empathy, negotiation, compromise and positive assertion .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Plan the environment to create spaces for children to play alone, alongside or with others.
• Provide time, space and open-ended materials for children to collaborate with one another.
• Create opportunities for children to get to know everyone in the group.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Represents and recreates what they have learnt about social interactions from their relationships with close adults.
• Develops particular friendships with other children.
• Is increasingly socially skilled and will take steps to resolve conflicts with other children by negotiating .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Support young children's efforts to join in with others' play and inviting others into their play.
• Offer calm and considered support for children as they experiences conflict with their peers.
• Recognise and respect children's particular friendships .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Provide play activities that encourage cooperation and collaboration.
• Choose books, puppets, and dolls and small world play that help children explore their ideas about friends.
• For young children who are finding it hard to make relationships, develop other situations such as forest school.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Learns about their physical self through exploratory play with their hands and feet.
• Is becoming aware of self as they imitate sounds and expressions.
• Shows awareness of being a separate individual through initiating contact with others .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Engage in attentive, uninterrupted play with babies when they are alert and ready.
• Provide many opportunities for babies to explore how their bodies move.
• Listen, respond to and build on babies' expressions, actions, and gestures .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Allow for flexibility within practice so that the routines you follow offer continuity.
• Learn from parents/carers about each baby's family culture, traditions and languages.
• Provide comfortable areas where parents, practitioners and young babies can be together.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Expresses awareness of their physical self through their own movements, gestures and expressions.
• Shows growing confidence that their needs will be met by freely expressing their need for comfort.
• Responds to their own name and enjoys finding own nose, eyes or tummy .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Spend one-to-one time playing, talking and looking at books that are of personal relevance.
• Talk with babies about people and things that are special to them.
• Offer commentary to babies about what is happening around them .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Place mirrors where babies can see their own reflection.
• Create sufficient safe space for babies to move, roll, stretch and explore.
• Provide objects and images that reflect the baby and their home.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Is aware of and interested in their own and others' physical characteristics.
• Experiments with what their bodies can do through setting themselves physical challenges.
• Begins to use me, you and I in their talk .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Use play and stories to positively support toddlers' understanding of their physical selves.
• Share toddlers' pleasure when they do something for themselves.
• Recognise a child's growing sense of agency and respect their attempts to gain independence .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Create displays and albums of photographs of the children and the activities they have participated in.
• Encourage children to take their own photographs within the setting.
• Displays, equipment and resources are reflective of the children's linguistic social and cultural backgrounds.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Knows their own name, their preferences and interests and is becoming aware of their unique abilities.
• Is developing an understanding of and interest in differences of gender, ethnicity and ability.
• Shows a sense of autonomy through asserting their ideas and preferences .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Provide toddlers with opportunities to practise making choices and decisions.
• Support toddlers' autonomy by involving them in the daily organisation of the home or group.
• Be close by and available to provide encouragement and support when a toddler needs it .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Plan the environment so that storage for coats, nappies, shoes and comforters are labelled.
• Provide an environment that is stable and familiar so children can find what they need.
• Plan personalised play that follows each child's interests.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Is becoming more aware of the similarities and differences between themselves and others.
• Is sensitive to others' messages of appreciation or criticism.
• Enjoys a sense of belonging through being involved in daily tasks .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Celebrate each child's uniqueness by openly talking with them about their individual characteristics.
• Value difference through showing genuine interest in and valuing all children's contributions.
• Offer extra support to children in new situations or when they are feeling anxious .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Involve parents in their children's learning and learn about each child's home culture from them.
• Plan regular opportunities for children to talk to their small group about something they are interested in.
• Include mirrors and photographs of the children and their families and friends in the environment.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Recognises that they belong to different communities and social groups.
• Is more aware of their relationships to particular social groups and sensitive to prejudice.
• Shows confidence in speaking to others about their own needs, wants, interests and opinions .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Engage with children in exploring and talking about what they are doing, valuing their ideas.
• Offer help with activities when asked but not before and see struggle and mistakes as important parts of learning.
• Intervene when children need help and validation of feelings in difficult situations .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Give time for children to pursue their play and learning without interruption.
• Provide experiences and activities that are challenging but achievable.
• Provide a role-play area resourced with materials reflecting children's family lives and communities.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Communicates a range of emotions (e.g. pleasure, interest, fear) through making sounds and facial expressions.
• Expresses feelings strongly through crying in order to make sure that their needs will be met.
• Seeks physical and emotional comfort by snuggling in to trusted adults .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Learn from parents about how their baby expresses their emotions and what they do to soothe them.
• Support babies who are distressed on separating from their parents by acknowledging their feelings.
• Be responsive to all communication such as crying, babbling and physical movements .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Observe babies' emotional responses and plan the routines, the environment and play experiences to support them.
• Encourage parents to bring their baby's comforter/transitional object.
• Create a cosy, quiet place for babies to be calm.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Shows a wider variety of feelings, using crying, gestures and vocalisations freely.
• Begins to become aware of their emotions as the connections in the brain that make feelings conscious grow.
• Uses familiar adult to share feelings such as excitement and for 'emotional refuelling' .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Tune in to a baby's emotions and respond calmly, gently and sensitively.
• Use calming processes such as rocking or calmly singing in response to emotional expression.
• Learn lullabies and other songs that babies know from home .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Create spaces and experiences in which babies feel secure enough to explore and play.
• Provide resources including picture books and stories that focus on a range of emotions.
• Store babies' toys and comforters where they can find and reach them.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Expresses positive feelings such as joy and affection and negative feelings such as anger.
• Experiences a wide range of feelings with great intensity, such as anger and frustration.
• Is aware of others' feelings and is beginning to show empathy .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Be a secure base for toddlers to return to for 'emotional refuelling' when encountering novel situations.
• Create regular opportunities to be in very small groups or 1:1 times with the key person.
• Reduce frustration and conflict by keeping routines flexible .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Maintain consistency of key person relationships in the organisation of staffing.
• Keep changes in group and routine to a minimum.
• Ensure that observation and planning for children's emotional needs is a central focus.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Expresses the self-aware emotions of pride and embarrassment.
• Can feel overwhelmed by intense emotions, resulting in an emotional collapse.
• Is becoming able to think about their feelings as their brain starts to develop the connections .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Show empathy and stay close by to offer support and reassurance as the child calms after an emotional collapse.
• Use real life experiences to help children to understand a wide range of emotions.
• Model empathy and talk about others' feelings .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Provide books, stories and puppets that can be used to model responding to others' feelings.
• Provide sufficient materials and duplicates of popular items to reduce conflict.
• Create calm spaces inside and out, for retreat and relaxation.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Expresses a wide range of feelings in their interactions with others.
• May exhibit increased fearfulness of things like the dark or monsters.
• Talks about how others might be feeling and responds according to their understanding .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Create a listening culture and atmosphere which is calm and caring.
• Name and talk about a wide range of feelings and make it clear that all feelings are acceptable.
• Model how you manage your own feelings, e.g. I'm feeling a bit angry and I need to calm down .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Plan small group circle times when children can explore feelings, e.g. through stories.
• Provide photographs and books where emotions are being expressed.
• Use Persona Dolls to help children consider feelings and ways to help others feel better.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Understands their own and other people's feelings, offering empathy and comfort.
• Talks about their own and others' feelings and behaviour and its consequences.
• Is more able to manage their feelings and tolerate situations in which their wishes cannot be met .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Help children to recognise when their actions hurt others.
• Be emotionally available to young children when they need to 'emotionally refuel'.
• Support children in recognising the consequences of behaviours and responses .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Offer environments that include stimulating and challenging spaces but also calm and comfortable spaces.
• Set, explain and maintain clear, reasonable and consistent boundaries.
• Involve children in agreeing codes of behaviour and taking responsibility for implementing them.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Turns toward a familiar sound then locates range of sounds with accuracy.
• Listens to, distinguishes and responds to intonations and sounds of voices.
• Reacts in interaction with others by smiling, looking and moving .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Get physically close making sure the baby can see your face.
• Show that you are present and tuned in by using eye contact and touch.
• Be attentive and leave space for the baby to start a 'serve and return' conversation .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Share stories, songs and rhymes from all cultures and in babies' home languages.
• Share favourite stories, songs, rhymes or music as babies are settling to sleep.
• Create an environment which invites responses from babies and adults.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Moves whole body to sounds they enjoy, such as music or a regular beat.
• Concentrates intently on an object or activity of own choosing for short periods.
• Pays attention to dominant stimulus - easily distracted by noises or other people talking .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Imitate the baby's responses to show you notice and value their contributions.
• Encourage playfulness, laughter, turn-taking and responses.
• Sing songs and rhymes during everyday routines .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Consider what it feels like to use your voice in your environment.
• Collect resources that children can listen to and learn to distinguish between.
• Encourage listening in its widest sense; human noises, non-human noises, etc..

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Listens to and enjoys rhythmic patterns in rhymes and stories.
• Enjoys rhymes and demonstrates listening by trying to join in with actions or vocalisations.
• Pays attention to own choice of activity, may move quickly from activity to activity .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Follow the baby's focus and pay joint attention to what they are interested in.
• Use natural gestures and/or signing e.g. waving 'bye-bye'.
• Play alongside the child and talk together .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Provide opportunities to listen to the sounds of the local area.
• Listen to sounds that are easily identifiable and mysterious noises that are not.
• Use puppets and other props to encourage listening and responding.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Listens with interest to the noises adults make when they read stories.
• Recognises and responds to many familiar sounds, e.g. turning to a knock on the door.
• Single channelled attention; can shift to a different task if attention fully obtained .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Model being a listener by listening to children and taking account of what they say.
• Have conversations with children as part of everyday activities.
• Model and encourage language for thinking by using phrase such as I wonder... .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Encourage children to learn one another's names and to pronounce them correctly.
• Where possible minimise background noise and visual distractions.
• Encourage talk in all spaces, both indoors and outdoors.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Listens to others in one-to-one or small groups, when conversation interests them.
• Listens to familiar stories with increasing attention and recall.
• Joins in with repeated refrains and anticipates key events and phrases in rhymes .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Encourage repetition, rhythm and rhyme by using tone and intonation.
• Be aware of and actively support the needs of children learning English as an additional language.
• Engage in role play and imaginary play scenarios and model listening behaviours .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Plan activities listening carefully to different speech sounds, e.g. a sound chain.
• When singing or saying rhymes, talk about the similarities in the rhyming words.
• Set up a listening area or other opportunities where children can enjoy rhymes and stories.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Is able to follow directions (if not intently focused).
• Shows variability in listening behaviour; may move around but still be listening.
• May indicate two-channelled attention, e.g. paying attention to something of interest for short or long periods .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Cue children, particularly those with communication difficulties, to listen by first using their name.
• Share rhymes, books and stories from many cultures, sometimes using languages other than English.
• Invite parents and members of wider communities to story-telling opportunities .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Choose stories with repeated refrains, dances and action songs.
• Plan regular short periods when individuals listen to others, such as singing a short song.
• Play games which involve listening for a signal, such as Simon Says.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Turns when hears own name.
• Starts to understand contextual clues, e.g. familiar gestures, words and sounds .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Look at the baby and say their name.
• Interpret and give meaning to the things young babies show interest in.
• Use an animated, enthusiastic face when interacting with children .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Let babies see and hear the sequence of actions you go through as you carry out familiar routines.
• Provide resources and spaces that stimulate babies' interests.
• Find out from parents how babies make themselves understood at home.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Is developing the ability to follow others' body language, including pointing and gesture.
• Responds to simple questions when in a familiar context (e.g. Where's Mummy?).
• Understanding of single words in context is developing, e.g. cup, milk, daddy .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Observe children as they watch their environment.
• Talk to babies about what you are doing and what is happening, so they will link words with actions.
• Use actions including hands and finger plays to support your words .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Display lists of words from different home languages.
• When singing rhymes and songs use actions to support children's understanding of words.
• Plan play activities and provide resources which encourage young children to engage in symbolic play.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Understands different situations - able to follow routine events and activities.
• Selects familiar objects by name and will go and find objects when asked.
• Understands simple sentences (e.g. Throw the ball) .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Use gestures and facial expression to help show your meaning.
• Be aware that young children's understanding is much greater than their ability to express their thoughts.
• Use language appropriate to the child's level of understanding .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Plan real world shared experiences such as visits, everyday tasks.
• Use pictures, books, real objects, and signs alongside your words.
• Stay with the child while they play, taking time to watch their movements.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Identifies action words by following simple instructions, e.g. Show me jumping.
• Beginning to understand more complex sentences, e.g. Put your toys away and then sit on the carpet.
• Understands who, what, where in simple questions .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Be attentive and respond to children's talk in an appropriate and positive way.
• Use talk to describe what children are doing by providing a running commentary.
• Talk slowly enough for the child to understand .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Include things which excite young children's curiosity, such as hats, bubbles, shells.
• Provide activities, such as cooking, where talk is used to anticipate or initiate what children will be doing.
• Stay with the child while they play, play alongside the child and show attentive companionship.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Understands use of objects (e.g. Which one do we cut with?).
• Shows understanding of prepositions such as under, on top, behind.
• Responds to instructions with more elements, e.g. Give the big ball to me .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Prompt children's thinking and discussion through involvement in their play.
• Talk to children about what they have been doing and help them to reflect upon and explain events.
• When you need to give children directions be clear and help them to deal with those involving more than one action .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Set up shared experiences that children can reflect upon, e.g. visits, cooking, or stories.
• Help children to predict and order events coherently by providing props.
• Tune into children's preferred modes of communication.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Understands a range of complex sentence structures including negatives, plurals and tense markers.
• Beginning to understand humour, e.g. nonsense rhymes, jokes.
• Able to follow a story without pictures or props .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Ask children to think in advance and predict how they will accomplish a task.
• Use appropriate vocabulary during play with children to encourage them to think about stories.
• Use stories from books to focus children's attention on predictions and explanations .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Provide practical experiences that encourage children to ask and respond to questions.
• Alongside books, introduce story props, such as pictures, puppets and objects.
• Set up displays that are interactive so children can touch, pick up etc.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Communicates needs and feelings in a variety of ways including crying, gurgling, babbling.
• Makes own sounds in response when talked to by familiar adults.
• Practises and gradually develops speech sounds (babbling) .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Find out from parents how they like to communicate with their baby.
• Pay attention to babies' communications including facial expression, gesture, etc..
• Encourage babies' sounds and babbling by copying their sounds in a turn-taking interaction .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Learn and use key words in the home languages of babies in the setting.
• Value and learn from families about their communities, languages and cultures.
• Encourage parents to record familiar, comforting sounds, such as lullabies in home languages.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Points and looks to make requests and to share an interest.
• Uses sounds in play, e.g. brrrm for toy car.
• Frequently imitates words and sounds .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Communicate with parents to exchange and update information about babies' personal words.
• Try to 'tune in' to the different messages young babies are attempting to convey.
• Look out for patterns of communications they use to invite you into encounters .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Find out from parents the words that children use for things which are important to them.
• Explain that strong foundations in a home language support the development of English.
• Tune into what different children enjoy and create environments where babbling and talking feels easy.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Copies familiar expressions, e.g. Oh dear, All gone.
• Beginning to put two words together (e.g. Want ball).
• Uses gestures, sometimes with limited talk, e.g. reaches toward toy, saying Want it .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Share the fun of discovery and value babies' attempts at words.
• When babies try to say a word, repeat it back so they can hear the name of the object clearly.
• Build vocabulary by giving choices, e.g. apple or satsuma? .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Allow time to follow young children's lead and have fun together while developing vocabulary.
• Provide stories with repetitive phrases and structures to read aloud to children.
• Display pictures and photographs showing engaging, familiar or fantastical events.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Beginning to ask simple questions.
• Beginning to talk about people and things that are not present.
• Uses language to share feelings, experiences and thoughts .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Model building sentences by repeating what the child says and adding another word.
• Give the child enough time to talk with silences to allow the child to respond.
• Show children how to pronounce or use words by responding and repeating what they say in the correct way .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Provide activities which help children to learn to distinguish differences in sounds.
• Plan to encourage correct use of language by telling repetitive stories.
• Provide opportunities for children to communicate in their home language.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Holds a conversation, jumping from topic to topic.
• Uses a variety of questions (e.g. what, where, who).
• Beginning to use more complex sentences to link thoughts (e.g. using and, because) .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Play with sounds and words children use, such as nonsense language.
• Wait and allow the child time to start the conversation.
• Follow the child's lead to talk about what they are interested in .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Help children to build their vocabulary, motivations and opportunities to experiment with talk.
• Foster children's enjoyment of spoken and written language by providing interesting play opportunities.
• Plan regular opportunities for children to speak, e.g. take turns having a toy animal at home.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Uses talk to explain what is happening and anticipate what might happen next.
• Questions why things happen and gives explanations.
• Extends vocabulary, especially by grouping and naming, exploring the meaning and sounds of new words .
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Use lively intonation and animated expression when speaking with children.
• Talk with children to make links between their body language and words.
• Use a lot of statements and comments and fewer questions to build natural conversation .
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Provide small world toys or puppets for children to act out familiar stories.
• Set up collaborative tasks, e.g. construction, food activities or story-making.
• Provide opportunities for talking for a wide range of purposes, e.g. to present ideas.

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Gradually develops ability to hold up own head 
• Makes movements with arms and legs which gradually become more controlled 
• Follows and tracks a sound or moving object
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Ensure that from birth onwards babies have frequent opportunities for moving and being active 
• Take babies outdoors as much as possible 
• Give babies lots of time being touched and held
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• The caregiver's body is the first and foremost enabling environment 
• Provide comfortable seating both indoors and outdoors 
• Make the most of the outdoors for providing tactile and visual stimulation

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Belly crawling moves into crawling up on hands and knees 
• Becomes adept at changing position from crawling to sitting 
• Sits unsupported on the floor, leaving hands free
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Enable older babies to have at least three hours a day moving and being active 
• Develop a shared approach to managing risk 
• Ensure that clothing supports babies' mobility
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Alongside the continuing role of adult bodies, the floor is the best enabling environment 
• Limit the time older babies spend in seats 
• Plan space to encourage free movement

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Develops security in walking upright using feet alternately 
• Walks upstairs facing forwards holding rail or hand of adult 
• Changes position from standing to squatting and sitting with little effort
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Enable toddlers to have at least three hours a day moving and being active 
• Develop a shared team culture of managing risk positively 
• Continue to provide a visible, attentive 'safe base'
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Anticipate young children's exuberance and ensure the space is clear 
• Provide opportunities to swing, spin and bounce 
• Ensure that toddlers spend lots of time outdoors experiencing uneven ground

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Sits up from lying down, stands up from sitting and squats with steadiness 
• Runs safely on whole foot 
• Jumps up into the air with both feet leaving the floor
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Value the ways children choose to move 
• Give as much opportunity as possible for children to move freely between indoors and outdoors 
• Talk to children about their movements and help them to explore new ways
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Plan opportunities for children to tackle a range of levels and surfaces 
• Provide a range of large play equipment that can be used in different ways 
• Plan time for children to experiment with equipment

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Climbs stairs, steps and moves across climbing equipment using alternate feet 
• Walks down steps or slopes whilst carrying a small object 
• Runs with spatial awareness and negotiates space successfully
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Encourage children to move with controlled effort 
• Use music of different tempo, styles and cultures to create moods 
• Motivate children to be active through group games
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Provide time and space to enjoy energetic play outdoors daily 
• Provide large portable equipment that children can move about safely 
• Practise movement skills through games with beanbags, cones, balls

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Uses simple tools to effect changes to materials 
• Shows a preference for a dominant hand 
• Begins to form recognisable letters independently
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Notice a child who moves repetitively in a particular way 
• Notice a child who lacks strength in limbs to push, pull or move
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Provide access to waterproofs and wellington boots 
• Provide equipment that supports different kinds of schemas 
• Agree acceptable levels of risk and challenge

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Responds to and thrives on warm, sensitive physical contact and care 
• Makes needs known through crying and body movements 
• Sleeps for 14-16 hours a day, with several short naps

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:
• Compares two small groups of up to five objects 
• May enjoy counting verbally as far as they can go 
• Subitises one, two and three objects (without counting) 
• Counts up to five items, recognising that the last number said represents the total 
• Links numerals with amounts up to 5 and maybe beyond 
• Through play and exploration, beginning to learn that numbers are made up (composed) of smaller numbers
Positive Relationships (What adults migh:
• Encourage children to share items between two people or toys 
• Capitalise on children's fascination with counting by joining in when they count 
• Model and encourage counting and representing numbers within role play 
• When counting objects with children emphasise the cardinal principle 
• Emphasise the one more, one less pattern in rhymes and traditional tales
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Provide a numeral rich environment, e.g. in role-play areas 
• Provide resources indoors and outside for children to explore and talk about higher numbers 
• Model using objects to illustrate counting songs, rhymes and number stories 
• Play with either dot or numeral dice 
• Explore different arrangements of the same number, e.g. partitioning five in different ways

A Unique Child (What a child might be do:

• Support children in their problem solving when they are creating rail tracks and road layouts
Enabling Environments (What adults might:
• Provide opportunities for children to explore position themselves inside, behind, on top 
• Provide picture books to stimulate discussion about position and direction 
• Create trails and treasure hunts with the children
